title: Watch the Evolution of Manhattan Unfold in a Timelapse Video, from 1600 to 2026
description:
in Architecture, History |   	August 3rd, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

A Man­hat­tan with­out sky­scrap­ers sounds dif­fi­cult, if not impos­si­b
body:
in Architecture, History |   	August 3rd, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

A Man­hat­tan with­out sky­scrap­ers sounds dif­fi­cult, if not impos­si­ble, to imag­ine today. But such a place real­ly did exist, at least up until the turn of the twen­ti­eth cen­tu­ry. While the title of the very first sky­scraper ever built may go to the Home Insur­ance Build­ing in Chica­go, New York City caught up so aggres­sive­ly there­after — in its char­ac­ter­is­tic style — that it soon became prac­ti­cal­ly syn­ony­mous with tall steel-framed tow­ers. The shape of mod­ern Man­hat­tan would sure­ly have been unimag­in­able to the first non-native arrivals in the ear­ly sev­en­teenth cen­tu­ry, the approach of whose ships you can see re-cre­at­ed in the ani­mat­ed time­lapse above.
The video is a pro­duc­tion of CITY 3D TIMELAPSE, a YouTube chan­nel pre­vi­ous­ly fea­tured here on Open Cul­ture for its sim­i­lar­ly accel­er­at­ed visu­al­iza­tion of the evo­lu­tion of Paris. While that video had 23 cen­turies to com­press into a three-minute run­time, this new one on New York takes a leisure­ly-by-com­par­i­son eight min­utes to ren­der “just” 450 years or so of his­to­ry (at least after about twen­ty sec­onds spent in the native era’s mil­len­ni­um and a half).
But it also shows us the urban evo­lu­tion­ary process three times: the first zooms out to the whole of Man­hat­tan, the sec­ond focus­es on Low­er Man­hat­tan, and the third on Mid­town Man­hat­tan — a suit­able divi­sion, as any New York­er knows, for those mutu­al­ly incom­pre­hen­si­ble civ­i­liza­tions.
Even if we’ve nev­er set foot there, we may well know that even old New York was once New Ams­ter­dam. That Dutch colo­nial era, as depict­ed in the time­lapse, is when the city begins. There fol­lows den­si­fi­ca­tion and expan­sion under Eng­lish rule, the mar­itime infra­struc­tur­al build-out of ear­ly Amer­i­ca, the ambi­tious grid-lay­ing under the Com­mis­sion­ers’ Plan of 1811, the relent­less nine­teenth-cen­tu­ry indus­tri­al­iza­tion that imbued the city with the might its rep­u­ta­tion still retains, the rise of the sky­scrap­ers that shaped (and con­tin­ue to shape) its sky­line, and final­ly the “glob­al­iza­tion era” in which we find our­selves today. That “we,” of course, includes not just New York­ers, but urban­ites every­where, for the evo­lu­tion of New York pro­duced not just a city, but in many respects, the city: the mod­el by which so many metrop­o­lis­es have been inspired to get a bit of the action for them­selves.
Relat­ed Con­tent:
A 3D Ani­ma­tion Shows the Evo­lu­tion of New York City (1524 — 2023)
Watch a Time­lapse Video Show­ing the Cre­ation of New York City’s Sky­line: 1500 to Present
Immac­u­late­ly Restored Film Lets You Revis­it Life in New York City in 1911
Watch Man­hat­ta, the First Amer­i­can Avant-Garde Film (1921)
Ani­ma­tions Visu­al­ize the Evo­lu­tion of Lon­don and New York: From Their Cre­ation to the Present Day
Watch the Evo­lu­tion of Paris Unfold in a Time­lapse Video, from 300 BCE to 2025
Based in Seoul, Col­in Marshall writes and broad­casts on cities, lan­guage, and cul­ture. He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

title: Watch a Monumental Iceberg in Greenland Do a Somersault
description: Greenland, the world’s largest island, is also covered in one of the earth’s two ice sheets. The other cloaks Antarctica. Greenland’s encompasses
body:
Greenland, the world’s largest island, is also covered in one of the earth’s two ice sheets. The other cloaks Antarctica. Greenland’s encompasses around 80 percent of the nation’s land mass, spanning more than 650,000 square miles. But it’s also melting at an accelerating rate due to climate change, losing an annual average of 261 gigatonnes—one gigatonne is equivalent to 2.2 trillion pounds—contributing to rising sea levels that impact the rest of the world. And Greenland’s massive icebergs are a reminder of this exceptional scale.
On July 25, a mammoth iceberg literally made waves as it flipped over off the coast of Ilulissat, Greenland. A video taken from town went viral online, and AfarTV, which has a livestream camera set up near the entrance to the UNESCO World Heritage-listed Ilulissat Icefjord, captured the event in high definition. “Large icebergs can remain grounded or trapped near the mouth of the icefjord while they melt, fracture and become small enough to move into Disko Bay,” AfarTV says. “It is not known precisely when this particular iceberg originally separated from the glacier.”

title: Inspired by Fauna, Form Meets Function in Hilarious Pieces by Ceramika Matylda
description: After spending many years painting, Agata Iwaszkiewicz picked up a ball of clay for the first time at 41 and felt a change. “I knew I’d found what
body:
After spending many years painting, Agata Iwaszkiewicz picked up a ball of clay for the first time at 41 and felt a change. “I knew I’d found what I had been looking for,” she tells Colossal. “Working with clay felt completely natural. Ideas came effortlessly, and I immediately had a clear vision for what I wanted to build with my new business.” Ceramika Matylda was born.
The Gdańsk, Poland-based artist is particularly drawn to animals, especially dogs. Their playful, quirky, cartoonish faces and spaghetti-like limbs are both relatable and slightly unfamiliar, tapping into a sense of sentimentality and curiosity. “My newest collection of poodles was inspired by my own dog, Rudolf, who passed away recently,” Iwaszkiewicz says. “These pieces are incredibly personal to me—they’re my way of saying goodbye to him and celebrating the joy he brought into my life.”

For Ceramika Matylda, the artist focuses predominantly on pieces that are both sculptural and functional, such as jars, candleholders, and salt and pepper shakers. Increasingly, she’s branching out into pure sculpture, like the playful vignette of a horse leaping over a wave as it gives an octopus a lift.
“I like my work to be open to interpretation,” Iwaszkiewicz says. “There’s a lot of humor in it, a sense of playfulness, and I never take the world too seriously. At the same time, every piece reflects my own aesthetic and my personal idea of what beauty can be.”
See more on Instagram, and find originals in her Etsy shop.

title: Guggenheim Abu Dhabi Will Finally Open
description:
Daily Newsletter
                The long-contested museum has an opening date. Plus, V&A Museum workers strike, a Taipei milita
body:
Daily Newsletter
                The long-contested museum has an opening date. Plus, V&A Museum workers strike, a Taipei military settlement becomes an artist residency, and a documentary on protest photography. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            After 20 long years of delays and allegations of abuse against migrant workers, the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi has finally announced an opening date: December 11. Yay? Across the world, another major museum is just gearing up its labor battle. Unionized workers at the Victoria and Albert Museum’s East Storehouse location voted unanimously to strike, alleging insufficient time to use the toilet or drink water. All the world’s an Amazon warehouse, it seems. But not everything trends toward shit. Sometimes the reverse takes its course — as a former military settlement-turned-artist settlement in Taipei shows us. May we all head that way. — Lisa Yin Zhang, associate editor


	
		
			How a Former Military Settlement in Taipei Became an Artist Residency
		
	
	
		Tucked away in a small forested area on the banks of the Xindian River in Taipei City lies the Treasure Hill Artist Village. Founded by retreating soldiers in the 1940s, the former anti-aircraft base turned squatter settlement has been through a number of reincarnations. 
          Its latest form, launched in 2010, is as a so-called “living history,” where the descendants of its original inhabitants live side by side with artists in residence. | Andrew Nachemson
	
	
		Read More
	

NewsAfter 20 years of delays, allegations, and recalibrations, the Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation will open the doors to its Frank Gehry-designed Abu Dhabi outpost on December 11.The new exhibition Help Wanted / Leave Now traces “Operation Wetback," one of the United States's worst deportation campaigns against undocumented Mexican workers.Unionized workers at the Victoria and Albert East Storehouse, a publicly accessible museum storage site, vote unanimously to strike over alleged “Amazon-style” working practices.Film Review

title: Michelle Grabner Donates More Than 2,000 Artworks to Wisconsin’s Kohler Arts Center, Now the Most Comprehensive Repository of Her Work
description: Artist Michelle Grabner will donate more than 2,000 artworks to the John Michael Kohler Arts Center (JMKAC) in Sheboygan, Wisconsin, making the inst
body:
Artist Michelle Grabner will donate more than 2,000 artworks to the John Michael Kohler Arts Center (JMKAC) in Sheboygan, Wisconsin, making the institution the most comprehensive repository of her work.

	Comprising 700 paintings, 200 sculptures, and 1,200 prints, Grabner’s gift spans the arc of her career, so far, with pieces made in the early 1990s to ones made in the past few years. Her gift also includes 300 works from her personal art collection, amassed via a combination of trades, gifts, and purchases, as well as her teaching materials and syllabi from her three-decade tenure at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago.
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	Grabner was born in Wisconsin in 1962, and she said growing up she was aware of the work being done at the JMKAC, which between 1972 and 2016 was led by Ruth DeYoung Kohler II. “Ruth was doing some amazing things there,” Grabner said, but when she was starting out as an artist in the 1980s, “what Ruth was doing was not what was compelling me.” Instead, she was looking to the art scenes in New York and Chicago, and “I wasn’t appreciating what was in my own backyard.”

	Beginning with DeYoung Kohler, JMKAC, Grabner said, has “an exceptional history of taking on artists’ environments that they collect, and they collect in mass, where the truth of an artist’s arc, their life, can be represented. They don’t just need the best Michelle Grabner. They have the resources to take on the full arc of the work, including archives, and that is exceptional.”


			
			
			
	
			
					Michelle Grabner, untitled, 2023.
									Photo Matthew Herrmann/©2026 Michelle Grabner/Courtesy the artist and Norr Cohan, New York
	



	That opportunity was exciting to Grabner as most museums are often focused on acquiring a single representative work from a specific moment in her career as opposed to having a more in-depth approach, especially for a mid-career artist like herself. Her work is held in a number of institutional collections, including the Art Institute of Chicago, the Walker Art Center, the Dallas Museum of Art, the Smithsonian American Art Museum, and the Victoria and Albert Museum, London. But now, the JMKAC “will become the principal institutional home for Grabner’s work and teaching archives,” as a press release put it.  

	The breadth of the gift grew out of several conversations with the JMKAC team, including executive director Amy Horst and chief curator Jodi Throckmorton. “The Arts Center was trying to think about how they could support me in this gift, and I said, ‘You would be supporting me by taking on my material mass,” she said, noting that she told them, “What you are giving me is an opportunity not to spend the last part of my life being an administrator of my own work.”  
	

	She continued, “I don’t have to worry about that. I can keep making work. I can keep making opportunities for other artists. I can keep that momentum going instead of arresting myself to thinking about, what is the value of these works? Where should they go?”


			
			
			
	
			
					Michelle Grabner, Patterns and Practicalities (continuation), 2020–21.
									Courtesy John Michael Kohler Arts Center
	



	“That Grabner is a Wisconsin artist with international significance makes this gift especially meaningful—it ensures that a practice with global reach remains rooted in the place that shaped it,” Throckmorton said in a statement, noting that the gift, which will now be accessible to the public, “allows us to work directly with Grabner to shape how her legacy is presented—how the work is shown, contextualized, and understood for years to come.”

	Though she still maintains a residence in Chicago, Grabner moved back to Milwaukee in 2015 and soon entered the Kohler orbit. She was invited to participate in Kohler Co.’s three-month Arts/Industry residency in 2017, curated an exhibition at the JMKAC in 2018, and in 2021 was commissioned to make a functional washroom for the JMKAC’s Art Preserve. In 2025, she participated in the Kohler MakerSpace residency program, where she made work in vitreous china. She currently serves as a curator for the Kohler Co.’s Arts/Industry Collection.
	

	Grabner said that her time as an Arts/Industry fellow was especially impactful on her practice. “It’s an exceptional residency—a super labor-intensive residency,” she said, noting it gets artists “to start thinking about both the idea that any variation from a Kohler line of products is a problem, but for artists, variation is interesting, so that works against it. It’s interesting to measure oneself against kind of industrial processes of sameness and efficiency [since] artists often talk about originality or variation in our work, so to deal with that on a daily basis while you’re working your ass off [is] exciting, quite draining, but also intellectually fascinating.”


			
			
			
	
			
					Michelle Grabner, untitled, 2023.
									Photo Matthew Herrmann/©2026 Michelle Grabner/Courtesy the artist and Norr Cohan, New York
	



	Grabner received her MFA from Northwestern University in 1990 and, since 1996, she has taught at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago (SAIC), where she is now chair of the Department of Painting and Sculpture. She sees the gift of her teaching materials as complementary to the JMKAC’s recent acquisition of the Roger Brown Study Collection, a semiprivate home museum made up of some 2,000 artworks by Chicago Imagists and other artists. Brown, who died in 1997, was a predecessor of Grabner’s on the SAIC faculty. The JMKAC collection also includes substantial holdings of the work of Barbara Rossi and Ray Yoshida, both of whom Grabner taught alongside at SAIC.
	

	Taken together, her gift and the JMKAC’s existing holdings of SAIC faculty, Grabner said, in a way shows the trajectory of the school’s Painting and Drawing Department and “how it was marked not only in pedagogy but also in aesthetic shifts in Chicago and what the sources of those artists were.”

	“This gift is so much more than the transfer of a remarkable body of work. It is an expression of trust built over years of relationship,” Horst said in a statement. “At the Arts Center, we’ve always believed that lasting partnerships with artists are at the heart of our mission and seeing that commitment returned in such a profound way is deeply moving. To be chosen as the permanent home for an artist’s life’s work is an honor and a reflection of our mission.”

title: Taryn Simon’s Guggenheim Show Will Fill Rotunda with Entirely New Body of Work for First Time in Museum’s History
description:
Taryn Simon’s upcoming solo exhibition at the Guggenheim Museum in New York will mark a number of firsts for the institution.

	Opening September 18
body:
Taryn Simon’s upcoming solo exhibition at the Guggenheim Museum in New York will mark a number of firsts for the institution.

	Opening September 18, the show will mark “the first time the Guggenheim has dedicated the entire rotunda to a new body of work and to a single artist working in photography and video,” according to a release.

	The exhibition, which will be accompanied by an artist book published by the Guggenheim and Hatje Cantz, has been in the works for nearly a decade and was initiated by Nancy Spector, the Guggenheim’s former artistic director and chief curator.
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	At the Guggenheim, Simon will debut Father Country I Do Love You (2026), a new body of work that lends the exhibition its title and consists of 42 chapters, a mix of photographs, texts, videos, and sculptures that she has not previously shown. The series centers on an “the real life of one unnamed federal agent” and his careers’ “labyrinth of sagas, in which Simon uncovers the ripple effects of her protagonist’s actions and inactions,” per a release.

	The release continues, “Through duty, devotion, loss, and happenstance, the federal agent acted as a middleman, witnessing events great and small and collecting evidence for someone else to slot into the bigger picture. Everything he touched ricocheted to the outer boundaries of nations and lives he’d never know.”

	Simon has dedicated Father Country I Do Love You to her father “whose life shadows the entire project. Her father lived in Thailand and traveled to Russia, Iran, Israel, China, Afghanistan, Korea, and elsewhere while working for the U.S. government, before transitioning to a career manufacturing and selling arcade games. Simon never got his full story, and, upon his diagnosis of Alzheimer’s disease, she realized she never would,” the release adds.

	“I’ve given birth to two children. Neither gestated for ten years in my guts. I could never have known what this would look like when it comes out,” Simon told ARTnews in an email. “When my dad still had language before Alzheimer’s, he said, ‘America is the best story on earth, if you could find someone to tell it.’”
	

	The Guggenheim Museum’s iconic rotunda, designed by Frank Lloyd Wright, hosts the bulk of the institution’s temporary exhibitions, often a mix of thematic and single-artist shows. Living artists who have taken over the rotunda include Carol Bove (2026), Rashid Johnson (2025), Jenny Holzer (2024), and Alex Katz (2022). One of the rotunda’s most famous exhibitions was Maurizio Cattelan’s 2011 retrospective, for which he suspended all of his past works in the center of the rotunda, leaving the walls blank.

	“Once again proving herself the consummate artistic storyteller of her generation, Simon has created a profound and personal body of work that rebounds between anxiety, survival, empathy, and play,” Nat Trotman, the exhibition’s curator, said in an email. “In Father Country I Do Love You, Simon shines a shaky spotlight on democracy, memory, and the invisible hands shaping the worlds we inhabit.”
